newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugoslavia needs new farm policy, better funding.
newsitem.headline: Yugoslavia needs new farm policy, better funding.

text.p: Yugoslavia urgently needs a fresh development strategy for its farming sector if it is to produce enough food for its population and achieve the targetted $2 billion in exports by the year 2000, experts said on Friday.

"If we want to enter international competition, the government must outline a new development policy for the sector," said Bora Djelovic, president of Jugoagrar, the association of agricultural producers.
"Agriculture must have special treatment in monetary policy. Conditions for financing production must be adjusted to the sector's capabilities and needs," he said.

The industry, burdened by high debts, shortage of cash, late wages, outdated machinery and low cultivation, mirrors the general poor state of the economy devastated by sanctions, war and mismanagement.

The sector helped the country survive difficult years of sanctions and war, it kept up production and fed the people but according to some analysts lost some $5 billion when funds were directed to other sectors of the economy.
Insolvency and lack of funds are the key problems in the sector which employs more than 70,000 people.

"Some people have not received their wages since last June," said Milutin Vucicevic, head of the Belgrade association of agricultural cooperatives. "And it is very difficult to force farmers to plant without paying them for old crops."

By mid-February Yugoslav farmers had not been paid some 800 million dinars ($143 million) for their 1996 crops but were expected to sow on 2.3 million hectares this spring. They are still owed some 100 million dinars.
"Above all stable and reliable sources of financing must be established," Djelovic said.

Jugoagrar called for a federal budget for agriculture to be set up to finance export-oriented production. Farm price subsidies and bonus payments should be introduced for some products. Customs levies could also be a source of financing.
Industry experts agreed 15 million dinars earmarked for agriculture support this year was not enough especially if producers were expected to sell abroad.
Ljiljana Vasic, head of the association of agricultural cooperatives in the country's bread-basket region of Vojvodina, said the state must decide if it wants to produce or import food.
"Agriculture accounts for some 30 percent of the country's gross domestic product (in 1996) which is a significant increase on the earlier eight percent," she said."
Dragoljub Sisic, a farmer from the central part of Serbia, said that after many generations, his son left farming due to difficult working conditions and low profits.

"Farmers must be treated and paid adequately because it is one of the most difficult jobs," Sisic said, adding, "the problem is that we do not trust the government any more. They should...do much more if they want to have enough food to feed the people." --Gordana Kukic, Belgrade Newsroom +381 11 222 4254
